faqs.a: They are invisible Unicode characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+FEFF) that take up no visible space. They sneak in when copying text from PDFs, websites and chat apps, and they can break search, sorting and password matching.
Four are handled: zero-width space (U+200B), zero-width non-joiner (U+200C), zero-width joiner (U+200D) and the byte order mark (U+FEFF). Each can be toggled on or off.
faqs.q: Which invisible characters does the tool remove?

faqs.a: Yes. Zero-width joiner (U+200D) is a legitimate part of many emoji sequences (like family emojis) and some scripts. If your text uses those, turn off the ZWJ toggle to keep them.
faqs.q: Could removing these characters break my emojis?

faqs.a: The byte order mark (U+FEFF) at the start of a file or text can confuse CSV importers and some programming tools. Removing it is the standard fix.
faqs.q: What is the byte order mark and why remove it?

zero-width-character-remover.formula:
For each enabled character class (ZWSP U+200B, ZWNJ U+200C, ZWJ U+200D, BOM U+FEFF):
  found[class] = count of occurrences in input
  output = input with every occurrence of each enabled class deleted
removed = input.length - output.length

limitations: Zero-width joiner (U+200D) is legitimate inside emoji sequences — keep its toggle off if your text contains such emojis.
The tool only targets the four listed characters; other invisible characters (like soft hyphens U+00AD) are left alone.
Removing the byte order mark changes file semantics for some legacy tools that expect it.
Counts are per character type, not per position — you cannot see where in the text they were.

zero-width-character-remover.workedExample:
Demo input (4 hidden characters): "he" + ZWNJ + "l" + ZWNJ + "lo, wor" + ZWJ + "ld" + BOM

Step 1: scan input -> ZWSP (U+200B): 0, ZWNJ (U+200C): 2, ZWJ (U+200D): 1, BOM (U+FEFF): 1
Step 2: all four toggles are on, so delete every occurrence of each enabled class
Step 3: input length 16 (12 visible + 4 hidden) - output length 12 = 4 characters removed

Output: "hello, world"

If the ZWJ toggle were off, the zero-width joiner would stay and only 3 characters would be removed.
mistakes: Assuming it removes every invisible character — it targets four specific ones; other oddities can survive.
Running it on emoji — removing zero-width joiners breaks family and profession emoji into separate people.
Cleaning Arabic, Hindi or Devanagari text carelessly — zero-width joiners shape these scripts, and stripping them corrupts words.
Re-pasting from the same source — if the source app injects the characters, they come right back; fix the source.
Assuming invisible characters were the bug — sometimes the real problem is encoding, and cleaning changes nothing.
